newsitem.title: MAURITIUS: EU sugar head sees ACP protocol price down by 2003.
newsitem.headline: EU sugar head sees ACP protocol price down by 2003.

text.p: The head of the Sugar Division of the European Union (EU) sees a future drop in the price at which the African, Caribbean and Pacific (ACP) states export sugar to the EU under the Sugar Protocol.
"From the year 2002 or 2003, we might reach a point where we might reduce prices," EU Sugar head Ejner Stendevad said during a talk in the Mauritian town of Reduit on Monday.
He said such price reduction would be at a rate of 3.3 percent per year over the next six years from then on the assumption that world sugar prices remained the same.

Under the Sugar Protocol established together with the Lome Convention in 1975, ACP states enjoy an annual export quota of 1.3 million tonnes to the EU at guaranteed prices well above world market prices.
The Protocol will outlive Lome which runs out in the year 2000 and quotas will remain after that date. But guaranteed prices will no longer be in the wake of world trade reforms.

"We believe there are difficulties ahead but other elements can come up till then. Here, we are speaking of unchanged world market prices. In a new world order with unrestricted access to markets, prices might go up as well," Stendevad said.
"The Protocol is not under threat. It is incorporated in the GATT (General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade)," Stendevad said.

He added there was a six year grace period in the GATT system and urged producers to use it to increase production efficiency by modernising production infrastructures, gear up research, improve irrigation systems and motivate cane growers.

The Indian Ocean island of Mauritius is the largest sugar supplier to the EU under the Protocol with an annual quota of 508,000 tonnes. Raw sugar makes up 450,000 tonnes of the quota and is exported at 537.70 Ecus per tonne to the EU.
Stendevad said Mauritius was already on track to face the prospect of lower future prices. "Efficient producers will take up the challenge and I view Mauritius as an efficient producer."

The Mauritian sugar sector invests some 400 million rupees ($19.3 million) per year in modernising. The industry is also awaiting a government policy paper on centralisation whereby the number of sugar mills in the island will be cut to 13 or 14 from 17 by the year 2000.

The Mauritian sugar industry will benefit from economies of scale by the rationalisation exercise, thereby lowering production costs and increasing productivity "Within the grace period, I am sure Mauritius would do well in its rationalisation," Stendevad said. ($1=20.70 Mauritian rupees). --Port Louis ++230 212-6870.
